passage: My name is Leela, and I was only passing through Howrah that Sunday, a visitor with one small bag and a train to catch. The announcement changed our platform, and the whole hall seemed to tilt towards the stairs. I stood by a pillar and watched. Most people simply shuffled, holding children's wrists, waiting their turn. Three or four men elbowed through, shouting, and a porter's trolley tipped. Then I noticed a young woman in a green dupatta, Rehana, I later heard her friend call her. She did not push. She steered an old man with a cane towards the second staircase, the one nobody was using, and pointed others to it too. I cannot say what she felt. Her face looked almost bored. I followed her down that staircase and reached the train with minutes to spare.

qa.q: Which staircase did Rehana guide the old man towards?
qa.a: She guided him to the second staircase, the one nobody was using.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling while standing by the pillar, and what shows it?
qa.a: Leela seems uneasy but steady; stepping aside to a pillar and watching, rather than joining the rush, shows a calm, wary alertness.

qa.q: What could Leela take from this for the next crowded station?
qa.a: Leela could stand still for a moment, look for a less-used exit or staircase as Rehana did, and keep an eye out for anyone slow or unsteady who needs room.

qa.q: How might Rehana's calm have looked to the old man with the cane?
qa.a: To him it was probably a relief: someone noticed he could be knocked over and quietly gave him a safer path without any fuss.

grounding: It illustrates a visitor watching a station crowd where most wait patiently, a few push, and one person's calm, eye for another exit and help for an elderly man stand out.

passage:
Friday. Nazia, visiting her cousin Kiran in Chennai for the first one-day match of her life, read the stadium map on the bus and circled the two gates nearest their stand. Kiran laughed at her. "It's cricket, not an exam."
Saturday. At the final over the crowd rose, and after the last ball everyone moved at once. Near Gate 6 a few boys started shoving, and a girl of about seven lost her father's hand. Nazia planted her feet, held the child's shoulder against the railing, and called out until the father pushed back through. Most people around them simply slowed and made space. Nazia then led Kiran to Gate 9, the one she had circled, which was half empty.
Sunday. Over filter coffee Kiran asked for the map. "Next time you mark the gates for both of us," Kiran said, folding it into a wallet.

qa.q: Which gate did Nazia lead Kiran to after the match?
qa.a: She led Kiran to Gate 9, the one she had circled, which was half empty.

qa.q: How might Nazia have felt when the girl lost her father's hand, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was probably alarmed but determined; she planted her feet, held the child against the railing and kept calling until the father came back.

qa.q: Which of Nazia's habits helped most in the crowd, and why?
qa.a: Circling the exits beforehand meant she did not have to think under pressure, and staying still with the child kept a small person from being swept along.

qa.q: How did Kiran's view of Nazia's map change over the three days?
qa.a: On Friday Kiran laughed at it, but by Sunday Kiran wanted it and asked Nazia to mark gates for both of them, showing new respect for planning ahead.

grounding: It illustrates a visitor at a match who finds most of the crowd patient, a few pushing, and relies on knowing the exits and helping a lost child.

passage: Aadhya, sit, you're going to the big mela with your office friends, so let your Nirmala Paati tell you something. I was twenty-four when I first went to a big temple festival in Madurai, on my own for the first time. When the chariot came round, the lane squeezed like toothpaste. Most people were gentle, you know. They folded their hands and waited. But two or three young fellows kept ramming forward, and one old lady beside me went down on her knees. I was frightened, I won't lie. My heart was running. But I remembered my father's voice: stand like a tree, look for the open side. I stood firm, pulled her up by both elbows and backed us into a shop doorway until the chariot passed. She gave me a jasmine string from her basket. I have never forgotten her face.

qa.q: Where did Nirmala take the old lady to wait until the chariot passed?
qa.a: Nirmala backed them into a shop doorway until the chariot passed.

qa.q: How did Nirmala feel when the old lady fell, and what did she draw on?
qa.a: She was frightened, with her heart running, but steadied herself with her father's advice to stand like a tree and look for the open side.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: The turning point was choosing to stand firm and pull the old lady up instead of being carried on; the doorway gave them a safe, open side away from the push.

qa.q: How might the old lady have experienced that moment in the lane?
qa.a: She was probably terrified on her knees in a moving crowd, and then deeply grateful that a stranger lifted her and kept her safe, which is why she gave the jasmine string.

grounding: It illustrates a young visitor at a temple festival noticing a mostly patient crowd with a few pushing, and using calm, an eye for an open side and help for an elderly woman.

passage:
Note for Sahil's parents from the after-school carer, Tuesday.
Around 5:10 the boys were playing cricket in the lane. Sahil hit a full toss and it went straight through Mrs Fernandes's kitchen window. I saw him drop the bat and run into the stairwell. When I found him behind the meter boxes, he was shaking and said Mridul had hit it. Mridul looked stunned. I did not scold. I sat on the step and said, "I saw the shot, Sahil. You're not in trouble for being scared." After a long silence he whispered that it was his. He said sorry to Mridul first. I phoned his mother, and at seven she walked him to Mrs Fernandes's door. Mrs Fernandes showed him the glass and let him help his mum sweep it up.

qa.q: Whose window did the ball break?
qa.a: It broke Mrs Fernandes's kitchen window.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when he hid behind the meter boxes and blamed Mridul?
qa.a: He was frightened and ashamed; he was shaking, hid, and grabbed at blaming someone else before he could face it.

qa.q: How did the carer's approach help Sahil tell the truth?
qa.a: By sitting calmly, saying what they saw and telling Sahil he was not in trouble for being scared, the carer made it safe for him to admit it.

qa.q: How might Mridul have felt when Sahil blamed him?
qa.a: Mridul was probably shocked and hurt at being blamed for something he did not do, and relieved when Sahil owned up and said sorry to him first.

grounding: It illustrates a child who breaks a neighbour's window, hides and blames another child, then owns it and faces the neighbour with a parent.

passage:
Thursday night
I broke Kulkarni aunty's window today. The rubber ball went off my bat and CRACK. Everyone ran. I ran the fastest, into the garage. When Kulkarni aunty came out shouting, I heard myself say it was Sumit's hit. Sumit just stared at me. My stomach felt like stones all through dinner. I couldn't eat the dal. Papa noticed and asked what was wrong and I cried and told him everything, even the Sumit part. He didn't yell. He said, "We'll go together, now, not tomorrow." Standing at her door my knees shook. I said sorry for the window and sorry for lying about Sumit. She said breaking glass happens, but lying makes her trust us less. Then she gave me a biscuit, which was weird. I messaged Sumit sorry. He sent back a thumbs up. Sachin, you idiot. But I feel lighter.

qa.q: What did the narrator tell Kulkarni aunty when she came out shouting?
qa.a: The narrator said it was Sumit's hit.

qa.q: How did Sachin feel through dinner, and what shows it?
qa.a: Sachin felt guilty and scared; the diary says their stomach felt like stones and they couldn't eat the dal.

qa.q: What did Papa do that helped?
qa.a: Papa listened without yelling and took Sachin to the neighbour the same evening, so the apology happened quickly and together.

qa.q: How might Sumit have seen the whole thing?
qa.a: Sumit was probably hurt and confused at being blamed by a friend, and the later sorry message may have eased it, though trust might take a little time.

grounding: It illustrates a child who breaks a neighbour's window, hides, blames a friend, then faces the neighbour with a parent and apologises.

passage: The tennis ball Jyoti had wrapped in tape flew off her plank bat and smashed the small glass pane in Pandit ji's front door, right beside the village well. Jyoti ducked behind the haystack. When Pandit ji came out asking who, she pointed at Jagdish, who was holding the ball because he had fetched it. Jagdish's ears went red. He said nothing. That evening Jyoti sat on the charpai, not touching her roti, until her Dadi asked what was the matter. It all came out. Dadi wiped her hands and took Jyoti's wrist. They walked together across the lane in the dusk. At the door Jyoti said, "I broke it, not Jagdish. Sorry." Pandit ji frowned, then nodded slowly. "You came yourself. That counts." Dadi arranged for the glass to be fixed, and the next morning Jyoti went to find Jagdish before school.

qa.q: Where was Pandit ji's house?
qa.a: It was right beside the village well.

qa.q: Why did Jyoti leave her roti untouched that evening?
qa.a: She felt guilty and afraid about breaking the glass and blaming Jagdish, and the worry sat heavily on her.

qa.q: What should Jyoti say to Jagdish the next morning?
qa.a: She could tell him plainly that she blamed him because she was scared, that it was wrong, and that she has told Pandit ji the truth.

qa.q: How did Pandit ji see Jyoti's visit?
qa.a: Pandit ji was annoyed about the glass but respected that she came herself to own it, saying that counts.

grounding: It illustrates a child who breaks a neighbour's glass, hides and blames another child, then goes with her grandmother to say sorry.

passage: Daniel had just found the chorus on his electric guitar when the knock came. Mr Chidi Eze from downstairs stood there in his security-guard uniform, eyes red. "Son, I work nights. Every afternoon, it comes through my ceiling." Daniel's face went hot. Every afternoon? He practised one hour. Other flats had dogs, babies, a man who drilled on Sundays. Why was it always him? He almost shut the door. Instead his mum, drying a pan, asked what times Mr Eze slept. Nine till three, he said. Daniel stared at the floor. "I could play after four," he muttered. "And with headphones before that." Mr Eze's shoulders dropped. "That would help me a lot." Next week Daniel left a note under his door: amp off till four. It came back with a smiley face drawn on it and the word thanks.

qa.q: What hours did Mr Eze sleep?
qa.a: He slept from nine till three.

qa.q: Why did Daniel almost shut the door on Mr Eze?
qa.a: He felt unfairly singled out and defensive, because other flats made noise too and he only practised for an hour.

qa.q: What made the compromise work?
qa.a: Asking about Mr Eze's sleep hours turned the complaint into facts, and a clear time plus headphones respected both Daniel's practice and the neighbour's rest.

qa.q: What is it like for Mr Eze when the guitar comes through his ceiling?
qa.a: After working nights he is exhausted, so noise during his sleep feels hard to bear, and Daniel's offer brings him real relief.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager who feels targeted by a neighbour's noise complaint and reaches a compromise on time and volume.

passage: The cricket nets at the Shivaji Nagar community centre back onto a row of houses, and on Monday Rafiq sir, the centre's manager, called Avni and her team into his office. "Mrs Bhatia has complained three times," he said. "The ball hits her wall at two o'clock, when her grandson naps." Avni folded her arms. "Then why is it only us? The football boys shout louder." She could feel her voice shaking. Rafiq sir did not argue. He slid a sheet across the desk. "Both of you have a right to be here. Write me a timetable you could live with." They did it right there: no batting against that wall between two and four, a softer ball on that side, and the loud warm-up moved to the far corner. On Friday, Mrs Bhatia sent a box of sweet biscuits to the nets.

qa.q: What time does Mrs Bhatia's grandson nap?
qa.a: He naps at two o'clock.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling in Rafiq sir's office, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt singled out and resentful; she folded her arms, pointed at the louder football boys and her voice was shaking.

qa.q: How did Rafiq sir handle the complaint well?
qa.a: He stated that both sides had rights and asked the team to write a timetable, which let them shape the solution instead of simply being blamed.

qa.q: What would change if Rafiq sir had just banned the team from the nets?
qa.a: Avni's team would likely feel punished and resent Mrs Bhatia, and the dispute would probably carry on in other ways instead of ending with biscuits.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager who feels targeted by a neighbour's noise complaint and settles it with a fair compromise on times and volume.

passage:
Dear Noor aunty,
Yesterday you told my mother the music from our balcony is too loud, and I'll be honest, I was angry. I went to my room and slammed the door. I thought you just don't like teenagers. It's my home too and it was only seven in the evening.
But then I remembered you mentioned your exams. You're studying for the nursing entrance, right? I didn't know that. So here's an idea. What if I keep the speaker indoors and low from six to nine on weekdays, when you study, and play it properly on Saturday afternoons? If something is still too loud, can you just knock or send me a message instead of going to Mum? I'd rather hear it from you.
Also, sorry about the Saturday night the song got stuck on repeat. That really was bad.
Nitin, flat 3B

qa.q: What times does Nitin offer to keep the speaker indoors and low?
qa.a: From six to nine on weekdays.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel when the complaint first came, and what changed it?
qa.a: Nitin felt angry and unfairly targeted, slamming the door, but remembering Noor aunty's exam study made the complaint feel more understandable.

qa.q: What makes this letter a good way to settle the problem?
qa.a: It admits the anger honestly, offers specific quiet hours and a fair time to play loudly, and asks for direct contact next time.

qa.q: How might Noor aunty feel reading this letter?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and respected, since Nitin noticed her exams and offered a plan instead of arguing.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager who feels unfairly targeted by a noise complaint and proposes a polite compromise on time and volume.

passage: Maria, you asked why I stopped parking under the neem tree, so listen. I'm Rajni, right, and you know I don't back down. There's one shady spot in our building and Mr Sehgal from the second floor had started leaving his car there every day. So I parked my scooter in it at six in the morning, just to make a point. He came down honking. I shouted. He shouted. For a week we were both sneaking out earlier and earlier, like idiots. I felt that if I moved, everyone in the building would think I was a pushover. Then the society secretary taped the parking chart on the notice board. The spot is for visitors. Neither of us. I actually laughed. Now Mr Sehgal nods at me in the lift and I nod back. Honestly, I'm glad the fight's gone.

qa.q: Where is the shady spot Rajni and Mr Sehgal fought over?
qa.a: It is under the neem tree in their building.

qa.q: What was Rajni worried would happen if Rajni moved the scooter?
qa.a: Rajni feared everyone in the building would think of Rajni as a pushover, so giving in felt humiliating.

qa.q: What finally settled the parking fight, and why did it work?
qa.a: The society secretary put up the parking chart, and a neutral rule that applied to both of them ended it without anyone having to lose face.

qa.q: How might Mr Sehgal have seen that week of early mornings?
qa.a: He was probably just as stubborn and irritated, feeling Rajni had taken his spot, and may have been quietly relieved when the chart gave him a way out too.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who treats giving up a parking spot as weakness, until the housing society's rule settles it calmly.

passage:
Monday: Darshan came home from college to find Tushar's family shoe rack and two bicycles blocking half the landing again. He dragged a cycle aside with a loud clang and snapped at Tushar through the door, "It's not your private room." Tushar snapped back. Darshan went in feeling hot and proud. If he let it go now, he told himself, they'd take the whole staircase.
Wednesday: Tushar's grandmother, who walks with a stick, stopped Darshan on the stairs. The rack was blocking her too, she said quietly. Darshan felt his anger shift into something more awkward.
Saturday: He knocked, this time without banging. "Can we sit with the society rules?" The printed bye-laws said landings must stay clear for safety. Tushar read them, sighed, and moved the bikes to the parking shed. Darshan helped carry them down. They ended up talking about cricket for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What did the printed bye-laws say about landings?
qa.a: They said landings must stay clear for safety.

qa.q: Why did Darshan feel he couldn't let the blocked landing go on Monday?

qa.q: How might Tushar's grandmother have been affected by the blocked landing?
qa.a: With her stick, the cluttered landing made the stairs harder and less safe for her, so the change probably felt like a relief.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who feels giving in over a shared stairway means weakness, but settles it through calm talk and the society's rules.

passage: Thomas, you think I was always this patient? Ha. When I was twenty-one, in Kochi, our lane had room for four scooters and there were six of us. Mr Varghese next door once parked across my gate, and I let the air out of his tyre. I was so proud of myself. The next morning his daughter had an exam and they couldn't leave. I watched from the window as they pushed the scooter to the pump, and his daughter was in tears. That changed something. That evening I went over, full of excuses, and ended up just saying sorry. Varghese chettan poured me black tea and we drew a little parking rota on the back of a calendar, whose day for the gate side. It hung in his kitchen for eleven years. Your uncle Hemant learnt more from that calendar than from college.

qa.q: What did Hemant and Mr Varghese draw the parking rota on?
qa.a: They drew it on the back of a calendar.

qa.q: What did Mr Varghese's daughter feel that morning?
qa.a: She was distressed and panicked about missing her exam, and was in tears as they pushed the scooter.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Hemant's story, and what made it work?
qa.a: Seeing the daughter in tears led Hemant to go over and apologise, and the rota on the calendar gave both families a fair, simple rule.

qa.q: How might Mr Varghese have felt when young Hemant came to say sorry?
qa.a: He might have been angry at first but also surprised and softened, since he poured tea and agreed to share the space fairly.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who treated a parking fight as a matter of pride, and a calm apology and fair rota that ended it without lasting bitterness.

passage:
Hi Sachin,
You asked about our society meeting. It was strange. About forty people came to the clubhouse, but only three spoke the whole two hours: the secretary, his brother-in-law and a man who owns four flats. They decided the lift repair, the watchman's hours and a new rule banning tenants from the pool, all in about ten minutes. The tenants sat at the back and stared at their phones. One aunty raised her hand twice and they spoke over her both times.
I almost left. Then I stood up, voice wobbling, and asked if we could have the rules and the minutes in writing before anything was voted on. It went very quiet. Then an old gentleman at the back clapped.
They agreed to circulate the minutes. I'll believe it when I see them.
Kamal

qa.q: How many people spoke during the whole meeting?
qa.a: Only three spoke the whole two hours.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel when standing up to ask for written rules?
qa.a: Kamal was nervous, with a wobbling voice, but determined enough to speak because the meeting felt unfair.

qa.q: What else could Kamal do to keep the meeting fair next time?
qa.a: Kamal could come again, sit with the quieter residents and support the aunty when she raises her hand, so more voices are heard.

qa.q: What would it be like for the aunty whose hand was ignored?
qa.a: She probably felt dismissed and small, and may stop trying to speak unless someone else backs her up.

grounding: It illustrates a young resident noticing that a few people dominate a society meeting and asking for written rules.

passage: Thanks, Himani, for having me on the campus podcast. So, I'm Hrithik, twenty-one, and the story is about my building. I started going to society meetings because my parents were travelling. First meeting, I just watched. Two uncles in the front row, same two every time, finished each other's sentences. Everyone else nodded or looked at the ceiling. One of them said, "It's always been this way," about a parking fee nobody had seen written down. And I noticed the ladies from the B-wing sitting completely silent. Later, one of them told me in the lift she'd tried once and been laughed at. So at the next meeting I asked, politely, for a copy of the bye-laws and a speaking list. The uncles were annoyed. But now the B-wing aunties speak. It's slower, messier, and much better.

qa.a: Asking politely for the bye-laws and a speaking list moved power away from a couple of loud voices and gave quieter residents a fair turn.

qa.q: How might the lady in the lift have felt about the meetings before the speaking list?
qa.a: She probably felt humiliated after being laughed at and unwilling to try again, so the list may have made her feel safer to speak.

grounding: It illustrates a young resident noticing that a few people dominate the society meetings while others stay silent, and asking for written rules and fair turns.

passage: I'm Ishita, and I sat three rows behind Asif uncle at the Green Park residents' meeting last month. I'll tell you what I saw, though I can't know what he was thinking. The committee chair talked for forty minutes about painting the gate. When the water shortage came up, Asif uncle raised his hand. The chair said, "Later," and moved on. Asif uncle lowered his hand and stared at his knees. He rubbed his thumb over a folded paper, what looked like a list of complaints from the old block. At the end, people rushed out. I went up to him and said, "Can I read your list?" He smiled, a little surprised. The next week I typed it up, and we both asked the committee, in writing, for water to be the first item. It was.

qa.a: He may have felt brushed aside and discouraged after preparing a list, and then surprised and grateful when someone younger took an interest.

passage: The Sunday yoga class in the Rose Colony community hall ended, and Aparna was rolling up her mat when she heard it from behind the pillar. "Comes back at midnight, every week. And that boy on the bike, who is he?" "Office, she says. Office till midnight?" Aparna froze. Her friend Trisha, beside her, raised her eyebrows and mouthed, "Want me to say something?" Aparna shook her head, cheeks burning. She walked out past the aunties and said, "Good morning, Sharma aunty, Dolly aunty," as warmly as she could. They went red. The next Sunday she brought a tin of banana bread for the class and mentioned, in passing, that her shift at the call centre ended at eleven and her colleague dropped her home. Dolly aunty asked for the recipe. The whispers about midnight stopped, mostly.

qa.q: When did Aparna's call-centre shift end?
qa.a: It ended at eleven.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel when she overheard the aunties?

qa.a: Greeting them warmly and later sharing plain facts left nothing to feed the gossip, whereas an angry reply might have given them a new story.

qa.q: How might Trisha have seen the moment behind the pillar?
qa.a: Trisha was probably indignant on Aparna's behalf and ready to confront the aunties, and may have been surprised by how steady Aparna stayed.

passage:
Dear Yamini,
You'll laugh, but I've become the colony's favourite serial. My mother's friend told her that people are saying I've "chosen someone from outside" and that's why I refused the proposal from Mehra uncle's nephew. Nobody asked me, of course. They just decided.
For two days I wanted to march over and tell them to mind their own business. I even rehearsed it in the shower. Instead I've been doing the opposite, which is harder. I say hello to everyone at the milk booth. When Mehra aunty asked, with that sweet voice, "So, any good news?", I said, "Not yet, aunty, I'll tell you first," and smiled. She didn't know what to do with that.
It still stings, honestly. But the stories get boring when I don't react.
Miss you. Write back.
Ishita

qa.q: What were people saying about Ishita?
qa.a: That Ishita had "chosen someone from outside" and that is why the proposal was refused.

qa.a: Ishita felt stung and angry, wanting to march over and even rehearsing what to say in the shower.

qa.q: What does Ishita's reply to Mehra aunty get right?
qa.a: It stays friendly and gives a light, open answer, so there is no defensiveness for the gossip to feed on.

qa.q: How might Yamini feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Yamini might feel protective and sympathetic, perhaps amused by the milk-booth moments, and glad to be the one Ishita confides in.

passage: Vikas, you know me, I'm Ayesha, I don't care what people think. Except I did. Last month the neighbour across the corridor told my landlord my friends were "coming and going at all hours." Four friends. Once. It was my birthday. The landlord called me and I felt about twelve years old again, being scolded. My first message to that neighbour was long and furious. I didn't send it. Thank God. Instead, the next evening I knocked with leftover cake and said, "Sorry if we were loud on my birthday. If it ever bothers you, please just tell me directly." She looked surprised, almost embarrassed. She said her husband works early. Fair. Now she waves when she sees me. My landlord hasn't called since. It still irritates me that she went around me. But I'm glad I didn't send that message.

qa.q: What did the neighbour tell the landlord?
qa.a: That Ayesha's friends were "coming and going at all hours."

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel when the landlord called?
qa.a: Ayesha felt scolded and small, like twelve years old again, and then furious enough to write a long angry message.

qa.q: What small step helped Ayesha most?
qa.a: Knocking with leftover cake, apologising for the noise and asking to be told directly turned a rumour into a real conversation.

qa.q: How might the neighbour have felt when Ayesha knocked on her door?
qa.a: She seemed surprised and a little embarrassed, perhaps expecting a fight, and may have felt relieved to explain about her husband's early work.

grounding: It illustrates a young person stung by neighbours' gossip about their friends who responds openly and politely rather than defensively.

passage:
Hi Vikas,
Remember how you laughed at me for knocking on every door in the building the week I moved in, with a plate of kaju katli? Well. Last Tuesday at 2 a.m. the pipe under my sink burst. Water everywhere, me in a towel, panicking. I called Mrs D'Souza downstairs because I had her number from the Diwali plate. She came up in her nightie with a torch and knew exactly where the main valve was. Her son brought buckets. By three we were drinking tea on her sofa.
And then, the funny part: two days later, the man on the fourth floor, the one who fights with everyone about parking, came to ask if the water had leaked into his flat. Because I knew him a little, we sorted it in five minutes.
So, I win.
Pallavi

qa.q: At what time did the pipe burst?
qa.a: At 2 a.m. last Tuesday.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel when the pipe burst, and what shows it?
qa.a: Pallavi was panicking, standing in a towel with water everywhere, and then relieved when Mrs D'Souza came up with a torch.

qa.q: What habit paid off for Pallavi, and how?
qa.a: Greeting neighbours with sweets when moving in meant Pallavi had a number to call at 2 a.m. and some goodwill when the fourth-floor man came to complain.

qa.q: How might the fourth-floor man have reacted if he did not know Pallavi at all?

passage: Madhav, you keep asking why I bother with the neighbours. Let me, Yamini, tell you about last monsoon. When I moved into the old building in Chennai, I did the dull stuff. Said vanakkam on the stairs. At Pongal I took a little steel box of sweet pongal to every flat, even to the grumpy man on the first floor, Mr Iyer. He barely said thanks. Then in July I slipped on the wet stairs and twisted my ankle, alone. Guess who heard me? Mr Iyer. He called an auto, came with me to the clinic, and waited two hours. A month later there was a fight about the water tank timings. Normally that meeting would have been a war. Mr Iyer stood up and said, "Let's hear the young lady." It was sorted in twenty minutes. That's why I bother.

qa.a: A little steel box of sweet pongal.

qa.q: What might Yamini have been feeling while lying on the stairs with a twisted ankle?
qa.a: Yamini was probably frightened and helpless, being hurt and alone, and then grateful and surprised when Mr Iyer came.

qa.q: What would you advise Madhav, based on Yamini's story?
qa.a: Madhav could try small, regular gestures, like greetings and festival sweets, even with grumpy neighbours, since goodwill builds slowly and helps in emergencies.

qa.q: How might Mr Iyer have felt about Yamini after the Pongal box?
qa.a: He may have felt noticed and quietly touched, even if he barely said thanks, which is perhaps why he helped and later backed her at the meeting.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult whose greetings, festival sweets and neighbourliness built goodwill that brought help in an emergency and eased a dispute.

passage: I'm Uma, from the flat opposite, so I watched Neelam's first year in our building. I can't say what was in her head, only what she did. She learnt everyone's name within a fortnight, even the watchman's children. On Eid she carried a tray of sheer khurma down the corridor. Then, in March, the new car-parking lines were painted and her car ended up half in Mr Rao's space. Mr Rao is famous for his temper. I waited for shouting. qa.a: He saw her as a good neighbour who had helped others, not as an intruder, so he felt relaxed enough to laugh and offer to repaint the line together.

passage: The night-shift break room at City Hospital was usually quiet, but on Thursday two ward assistants, Pramod and Salim, started arguing about who had left the laundry trolley blocking the lift. Within minutes it wasn't about the trolley. Someone from the corner muttered, "What do you expect from his lot?" and another person nodded. Pramod's friends drifted to one side. Salim's to the other. Joseph, a staff nurse eating idli from a tiffin, felt his stomach tighten. He had seen this before on the street near his house. He put down his spoon. "It's a trolley," he said loudly. "It's not anyone's community." Nobody laughed. Then he walked to the ward office and asked Sister Gargi, who both men respected, to come. She listened to each of them separately. By the next shift, a trolley rota was pinned by the lift.

qa.q: What were Pramod and Salim first arguing about?
qa.a: About who had left the laundry trolley blocking the lift.

qa.q: What did Joseph feel when the quarrel took on a community colour, and why?
qa.a: Joseph felt alarmed and uneasy, his stomach tightening, because he had seen this kind of labelling spread before on his street.

qa.q: Which of Joseph's steps worked, and why?
qa.a: Refusing the labelling out loud and bringing in Sister Gargi, whom both men respected, cooled the argument and brought it back to the trolley.

qa.q: How might Salim have felt when someone said "his lot"?
qa.a: He probably felt insulted and singled out for his community rather than his actions, which would make it much harder to calm down.

grounding: It illustrates an observer who sees a small workplace quarrel take on community colour, refuses the labelling and brings in a respected neutral senior.

passage:
Dear Yogesh,
Something happened in our lane this week that I keep thinking about. Two families fight over the common tap every summer. This Monday the fight was louder, and by evening a message was going round the lane group saying it was "their people versus ours". Photos, arrows, an old story about someone's grandfather. I got it forwarded to me six times.
I felt sick reading it. I know both families. Their kids play cricket together.
I didn't forward it. I wrote in the group, "This is about a tap, not about anyone's religion." Two people reacted with anger. One aunty messaged me privately to say thank you. Then my Nani and old Bashir chacha, who have both lived here forty years, called the two families to the temple courtyard and agreed a timetable for the tap.
It's calmer. I'm still shaky.
Disha

qa.q: Where did Nani and Bashir chacha call the two families?
qa.a: To the temple courtyard.

qa.q: How did Disha feel reading the forwarded messages, and why?
qa.a: Disha felt sick and upset, because Disha knows both families and their children play cricket together.

qa.q: What could others in the lane group have done to help?
qa.a: They could refuse to forward the message, add a calm reply like Disha's, and support the elders' meeting instead of taking sides.

qa.q: How might the aunty who messaged privately have felt?
qa.a: She was probably uneasy about the messages too but nervous to speak publicly, and relieved and grateful that someone did.

grounding: It illustrates an observer who sees a tap quarrel take on religious colour, refuses to join the labelling and supports neutral elders in settling it.

passage: So, Gurpreet, you asked what happened in my mohalla. I'm Madhuri, I was just coming home from work. A cricket ball hit a scooter mirror. Small thing. The scooter owner shouted, the boy's father shouted back, and suddenly someone yelled a caste name as if it explained everything. Boys started collecting on both sides. I felt my whole body go cold. I thought, this is how riots start in films. I didn't know what to do, so I did something stupid and simple: I walked into the middle and said, "Mirror costs how much? Let's just ask." People looked at me like I was mad. Then Masterji, the retired school principal everyone respects, came out in his vest. He sat both men on his steps. The boy's father paid for the mirror. Nobody said the caste word again, at least not out loud.

qa.q: What did the cricket ball hit?
qa.a: A scooter mirror.

qa.q: How did Madhuri feel when someone yelled a caste name?
qa.a: Madhuri felt frightened, the whole body going cold, fearing it could turn into something much bigger.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri's question about the mirror help?
qa.a: It pulled the quarrel back to the actual damage, a mirror, instead of the labels people were throwing, and gave everyone a practical way out.

qa.q: How might Masterji have seen the scene when he came out?
qa.a: He probably saw a small quarrel turning dangerous, and felt his role as a neutral, respected elder was to sit the two men down and calm them.

grounding: It illustrates an observer who sees a small quarrel take on caste colour and helps cool it with plain talk and a neutral elder.

passage:
Saturday, 10.40 pm
Posted my painting of the flyover at sunset at 6. Two hours of work, plus the week of sketches. First hour: 11 likes. I felt amazing. I checked while brushing my teeth, while eating, during dinner under the table. By 9 it was still 23. Pooja from class got 200 for a picture of her new shoes. I hate that I checked hers.
Around 9.30 I nearly deleted mine. It felt like proof that I'm boring.
Samir mama saw me refreshing and asked to see the painting. Not the phone, the actual paper. He looked for a long time and asked how I got the orange to glow. I explained the wet-on-wet thing. He said, "Twenty-three strangers pressed a button. I just spent ten minutes looking. Which counts more?"
I didn't delete it. Still checking though. Sharmila, stop.

qa.q: How many likes did the painting have by 9?
qa.a: It still had 23 likes by 9.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel around 9.30, and what shows it?
qa.a: Sharmila felt low and worthless, nearly deleting the post and calling it proof of being boring.

qa.q: What did Samir mama do that helped?
qa.a: He asked to see the actual painting and asked how it was made, showing real interest and gently pointing out that likes are not the real measure.

qa.q: How might Samir mama have felt watching Sharmila refresh the phone during dinner?
qa.a: He was probably concerned and a little sad, seeing how much the numbers were hurting, which is why he turned attention to the painting itself.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager who refreshes a post, feels proud at likes and low at silence, and an adult who gently shows numbers are not a measure of worth.

passage: Madhav's kabaddi raid had been perfect: two touches, a dive, a clean escape back over the line. His cousin filmed it behind the Barsana bus stand, and Madhav posted it that evening with loud music. Next morning, on the way to school, he checked the phone every thirty seconds. Eighteen likes. Then nineteen. By lunch he was proud and sick at the same time, because a boy from the next village had three thousand for a scooter wheelie. Madhav stopped talking during games period. Sarika ma'am, the PT teacher, noticed him sitting on the steps staring at the screen. She sat down with her whistle still around her neck. "Show me." He showed her. "Nice ankle hold," she said. "Now show me the part where you lost the last raid." He laughed despite himself. "Tomorrow," she said, "you teach the juniors that escape." He did.

passage:
Monday. The corridor dance was everywhere: the whole of 10B filming it on the wet back stairs after rain, sliding down the last three steps in socks. Devika watched Damini and the others practise and felt her face go warm when someone said, "You're not doing it?"

Damini had said, "No thanks, I'll hold your bag," and then held it. Damini also walked her to the class teacher, who sent her to the school nurse and banned filming on those stairs that same afternoon.

passage: Simran, you think these challenges are new? In 1989, when your Amandeep Bua was fifteen, the craze in Ludhiana was riding a bicycle with no hands down the canal bridge. Every boy did it, and then the girls started. I had never wanted to, not even a little, but Jaspreet and the others did it every evening and I stood watching like a lamp post. So one Sunday I did it. Halfway down my front wheel wobbled and I scraped my palms along the railing. I still have the mark, see? My friend Parminder had said, "No thanks, I'll wait at the bottom," and she waited, with her dupatta to wrap my hand. She walked me straight home, and my mother cleaned the cuts and asked why. I said, "Everyone was doing it." She said, "Parminder wasn't." That stayed with me.

qa.q: Where did the craze take place?
qa.a: On the canal bridge in Ludhiana.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep ride with no hands even though she did not want to?
qa.a: She felt left out standing and watching while her friends did it, and wanted to belong more than she feared falling.

qa.q: What was the key choice in the story that turned out wise?
qa.a: Parminder's choice to say no thanks yet wait at the bottom showed there was another way to stay part of the group without taking the risk.

qa.q: How might Parminder have felt waiting at the bottom of the bridge?
qa.a: She was probably nervous watching her friend and caring enough to be ready with her dupatta, and not at all less of a friend for saying no.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager joining a risky craze to fit in, and a friend who said no thanks and still stayed a friend.

passage: The school bus was leaving in ten minutes and it had started to drizzle. Rekha's group had decided this was the day for the new lip-sync trend: stand on the low wall by the railway footbridge, arms out, while a train passes behind. Everyone had one except Rekha and Kavitha. "Come on, Rekha, quick, before the train!" Rekha's heart thudded. She climbed onto the wet wall. It was slippery. She looked down at Kavitha. Kavitha shook her head. "No thanks. I'll film you from here, but I'm staying on the ground." Somehow that made it easier. Rekha climbed down. "Me too, from here," she said. The others groaned, then shrugged. The train roared past and they all danced on the pavement, laughing, rain in their hair. They got the bus with a minute to spare, and Kavitha sat next to her.

qa.q: Where did the group want to film the lip-sync trend?
qa.a: On the low wall by the railway footbridge.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling as she stood on the wet wall?
qa.a: Rekha felt nervous and pressured, her heart thudding, torn between wanting to fit in and knowing the wall was slippery.

qa.q: What helped Rekha change her mind?
qa.a: Kavitha's calm "No thanks" and offer to film from the ground showed there was a safe way to still take part.

qa.q: How might the others in the group have seen Rekha climbing down?
qa.a: They groaned at first, perhaps disappointed, but then shrugged and joined the pavement dance, which suggests they did not really mind.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager tempted to join a risky trend to fit in, and a friend whose no thanks shows fitting in has safer options.
